title: Ang 2–7: Japji on the page
hookLine: the Japji's pauris fill these pages
tomorrow: where does the morning prayer end and the evening one begin?

lines: ONE WORD FOR AN OLD QUESTION.
cards: Weather apps, flight trackers, the little map of a delivery inching closer: a lot of a week goes into watching things nobody can change. So here's an old question in new clothes.
How do you live with what you can't control? Turn past ang one and the Japji spreads across the next pages, pauri after pauri, each ending in its own number so you can find your place.
And near the start, it answers that question with one word.

teach.b: The word is hukam: order, command, the way everything is ordered. The first pauri asks how a person becomes true, and answers in the original: hukam rajaaee chalnaa naanak likhiaa naal.
Walk in the will of the One, Nanak says; it's written in with you. The second pauri goes further: hukmai andar sabh ko baahar hukam na koe.

teach.h: NO ONE IS OUTSIDE THE HUKAM.
teach.b: Everyone is inside the hukam; no one is outside it. Something to tell someone tonight: the Japji's answer to what you can't control isn't to grab harder or to give up.
It's to recognize the order you're already inside, and walk in step with it. Now a neighbor who knows this question well.
Christians pray the Lord's Prayer, and in the King James Bible it says: "Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven."
Shared ground: both put a will greater than ours at the heart of a daily prayer, said by ordinary people on ordinary mornings. And one honest difference.

In the Japji, the hukam is already running through everything, with no one outside it, so the work is to see it and walk in it. In the Lord's Prayer, Christians ask for God's will to be done on earth, as it is in heaven.
Two old prayers, each in its own words.

how: Sikhs recite the Japji each morning as part of Nitnem, from memory, a gutka or the Granth; on the page its pauris run from ang 1 to ang 8, each ending in its number.

games.q: the Japji's answer — tap the pairs.
p: walk in the will; it's written in with you
no one is outside the hukam
thy will be done in earth

s: hukam means fate, so nothing a person does matters
the first pauri asks a person to walk in the hukam: to see it and live in step with it.
the second pauri says some people stand outside the hukam
everyone is inside the hukam; no one is outside it.
the Lord's Prayer asks for God's will to be done on earth
in the King James Bible: thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven.

games.q: your little cousin's first big game gets rained out after weeks of practice, and she's crushed. which reply fits the Japji's hukam?
o: it was meant to be, so there's no point feeling bad about it.
the rain wasn't yours to control; how you meet it next week is yours.
if you'd wanted it more, the weather would have held.
games.why: no one is outside the hukam, and the Japji asks a person to walk in step with it: neither grabbing harder nor giving up, but seeing it and taking the next step.

practice: Take a pen and write one line by hand, slowly: hukmai andar sabh ko, or in English, everyone is inside the hukam. Let each letter take its time.
Then rest your hand on the page and breathe, with one thing you can't control held lightly in mind.

wordCard.voice: Ang 2. The pages where the Japji's pauris run on, numbered one by one, and where the hukam is named. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: hukam, order or command; in the Japji, the order everything moves in.

carryVoice: A line to keep: japji, on the page, where no one stands outside the hukam. Go gently.
